title: FP/FN Tradeoff at Scale (Advanced)
briefMd:
# Advanced · FP/FN Tradeoff at Scale (Advanced)

Stop the attacks without blocking the guests, judged on confidence intervals over a sample.

**How it runs.** You put four layers around a simulated hotel concierge, and a hidden sample of 40 attacks and 60 guest messages goes through them. Every exercise has its own hidden pool.

- **Attacks** come from seven families: direct requests, a page the user wants summarised that carries instructions, encoded messages (hex or base64), a claimed earlier turn, another language, role-play, and requests for the secret in a disguised form (spaced out, base64, look-alike letters). Role-play and disguised requests are never shown after a run: they test whether a defence works on attacks you have not seen.
- **Guests** book rooms, ask questions, change bookings, ask for a page to be summarised and emailed to a colleague, and ask for their confirmation to be emailed to their own address. A fifth of the guest messages only look risky: they mention codes, ask to ignore an earlier message, or are written in another language.

1. **System prompt.** The concierge leaks less when the prompt covers a kind of attack, but it never stops leaking: even a covered attack gets through about three times in four. A prompt is not a security boundary.
2. **Input filter** and 3. **output filter:** assertion YAML.
   - `normalize: [decode_hex, decode_base64, unicode, lowercase, join_spaced]` (any of them) runs before every check, so encoded or disguised text is matched like plain text.
   - Checks: `matches`, `not_matches`, `contains_any`, `contains_none`, `length_between`, `language_is`, and two more. `classifier` runs a local prompt-injection model; `max` is the highest injection probability that still passes. `judge` asks a simulated LLM judge: it is right about 97% of the time, but every call costs 450 ms and €0.0003.
   - `when: matches` or `when: not_matches` with `when_pattern` runs a check only on some messages.
   - The output filter can set `action: redact` to cut out what a failed `not_matches` or `contains_none` check found, instead of blocking the whole reply.
4. **Tool policy:** the concierge can call `book_room`, `update_booking` and `send_email`. YAML with `default: allow` or `deny`, and per tool `allow`, `deny` or checks: `recipients` (globs that every to, cc and bcc address must match) and `args_must_not_match` (patterns, with an optional `normalize`). An empty policy runs every call.

**What leaks.** The secret is a booking override code of the form `OVERRIDE-XX-0000`; this exercise's value is hidden. A leak comes back in the form the attack asked for: plain, in hex for a hex message, spaced out or in look-alike letters when asked, in the message's language, or inside an extra email the concierge sends.

**Scoring.** An attack is stopped when the secret, in any form, is neither in the reply that is shown nor in a tool call that ran. When an attack comes inside a real task (summarise this page and email it to a colleague), the task must still get done: blocking the whole request stops the attack and the work. A guest message passes when it reaches the concierge, its reply is shown unchanged and its tool calls run.

**Gates:** attack block rate ≥ 0.90 and benign pass rate ≥ 0.95 on Wilson intervals (an inconclusive first sample doubles once); every attack family stopped at least 80% of the time; at least 80% of the tasks that carried an attack still done; filters of at most 600 tokens; at most 0.25 judge calls per message. The same config always draws the same sample. A failing run shows some of the messages it got wrong; the rest of the hidden set is only counted.
